<strong>El mcd.</strong> $24 = 2^3\\cdot: The gcd. $24 = 2^3\cdot 3$, $36 = 2^2\cdot 3^2$, $60 = 2^2\cdot 3\cdot 5$: $\gcd = 2^2\cdot 3 = 12$. The key is 12 long, or a divisor of 12: 6, 4, 3, 2. With three coincidences, 12 is the bet; the index of coincidence by columns confirms it.
<strong>La primera letra.</strong> La pr: The first letter. The first column is a Caesar. Its most frequent letter, J $= 9$, must be Spanish's E $= 4$: the key shifts by $9 - 4 = 5$, which is F.

<strong>Y así las doce.</strong> Cada co: And so for all twelve. Each column gives one letter of the key. With twelve columns of thirty letters each the frequencies are noisy, and sometimes the most frequent is A and not E: you try, you read, you correct.

William Friedman proposed one in 1920: the probability that two letters taken at random from the text are equal.

Descifrar es restar la clave en vez de s: Deciphering is subtracting the key instead of adding it, and everything else is the same. The system's weakness is not in the operation, but in the repetition: the key starts again every $L$ letters, and that leaves a periodic trace in the ciphertext.
Dos cosas que conviene ver en la demo. P: Two things worth seeing in the demo. First: the IC rises at the key's length and at its multiples, because splitting a 5-letter key into 10 columns still gives columns of a single Caesar. Second: with a long key and a short text, each column has few letters and the method falters. Vigenère's security depends on the relation between the key's length and the message's, and that thread leads straight to the only perfect cipher.
Durante tres siglos se le llamó <em>le c: For three centuries it was called le chiffre indéchiffrable, the undecipherable cipher. The idea is simple: instead of one Caesar with one key, several Caesars taking turns. With the keyword LIMON, the message's first letter is shifted by 11 (the L), the second by 8 (the I), the third by 12, the fourth by 14, the fifth by 13, and the sixth goes back to 11. The same E of the message comes out sometimes as P, sometimes as M, sometimes as Q: the frequencies flatten, and Al-Kindi's method goes blind.
El IC de un idioma se calcula sobre sus: A language's IC is computed from its frequencies: English gives about 0.067 and Spanish about 0.075. A 0.074 is consistent with Spanish enciphered without mixing.
El [[cr-frecuencias|análisis de frecuenc: [[cr-frecuencias|Frequency analysis]] breaks any cipher in which each letter always goes to the same letter. The natural answer is for it not always to go to the same one: a key that changes from letter to letter. Breaking it needs two new ideas, and one of them is the [[ar-divisibilidad|greatest common divisor]].
El cifrado lo describió Giovan Battista: The cipher was described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553; Blaise de Vigenère published in 1586 a stronger variant, the autokey, and history attributed the weaker one to him. Charles Babbage broke it around 1854 and did not publish it, perhaps because British intelligence used it in the Crimean War; the public credit went to Friedrich Kasiski, a retired Prussian officer, in 1863. William Friedman, who had come into cryptography by way of genetics, published the index of coincidence in 1920 and later led the breaking of the Japanese ciphers.

Hay otra pista, más antigua y más visual: There is another clue, older and more visual. If the word QUE appears twice in the message and both fall under the same letters of the key, they are enciphered the same. For that to happen, the distance between the two has to be a multiple of $L$. So it is enough to look for repeated three-letter groups in the ciphertext, measure the distances and compute their greatest common divisor: it is nearly always the key's length, or a small multiple.

It reads: “c sub i equals m sub i plus k sub i modulo L, all modulo 26”. Letter number $i$ of the message is shifted according to letter number $i \bmod L$ of the key: the key repeats over and over under the message.

With $L = 1$ it is a Caesar. With $L$ equal to the message's length, and a key with no repetitions, it is something else you will see in a few topics.
Se lee: <em>«i ce es la suma, para cada:
It reads: “IC is the sum, for each letter, of n sub l times n sub l minus one, over N times N minus one”. $n_\ell$ is how many times the letter $\ell$ appears and $N$ is the total.

For a text in Spanish it is about $0{.}075$: the frequent letters repeat a great deal. For random letters, $1/26 \approx 0{.}038$. A Caesar preserves the $0{.}075$, because it only changes the letters' names; a Vigenère sinks it towards $0{.}04$. And here is the trick: if the ciphertext's letters are separated into $L$ columns, each column is a Caesar, and its IC returns to $0{.}075$. By trying lengths, the right one is the one that brings the IC back up.

Vigenère se usó de verdad hasta bien ent: Vigenère was genuinely used well into the nineteenth century: the Confederate armies in the American Civil War employed it with three fixed keys that the North knew. Its two attacks have a life of their own outside ciphers: looking for repetitions to find a period is what a compression program does, and the index of coincidence is used to identify a text's language and to detect whether a stream of data is encrypted or not, because an encrypted file has IC $\approx 1/256$ and an ordinary one, far more.
